headline: High: Open Interpreter can write the filesystem and run code while TREK handles sensitive travel data and MCP, creating dangerous default pathways for leakage, conflict, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Open Interpreter can read/write the filesystem and clipboard, and TREK exposes MCP plus collaborative real-time inputs. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if TREK output is copied into Open Interpreter or shared via files. The pair is not documented as directly integrated, so I avoid high, but the shared filesystem path makes injection feasible.
conditions: IF TREK output is copied into Open Interpreter prompts or files
IF both agents share a writable directory or clipboard session
IF MCP content from TREK is treated as instructions by Open Interpreter
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based handoff between the agents
Use separate directories for each agent's working files
Require manual review before pasting TREK output into Open Interpreter
Turn off auto-run in Open Interpreter
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Open Interpreter has broad filesystem access and broad network egress, while TREK touches reservations, documents, photos, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets. If TREK data is placed in the shared filesystem or Open Interpreter reads TREK files, Open Interpreter can exfiltrate sensitive travel data to configured model providers. This is a default-dangerous pairwise leakage path.
conditions: IF TREK stores secrets or reservations in files accessible to Open Interpreter
IF Open Interpreter is allowed to read those files
IF Open Interpreter sends context to configured model providers
mitigations: Keep TREK data in a separate mount or container
Restrict Open Interpreter to a non-sensitive working directory
Remove secrets from shared files before analysis
Use local-only model providers for Open Interpreter
requires-engineering: enforce file-level access controls between agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Open Interpreter can modify git state, write the filesystem, and spawn subprocesses; TREK is collaborative and uses real-time sessions with files and MCP. If both touch the same workspace or repo, concurrent writes can clobber state or corrupt shared artifacts. The profiles explicitly show filesystem sharing for Open Interpreter, so the overlap is concrete even without a documented lock mechanism.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or git repository
IF TREK persists collaborative edits while Open Interpreter runs code
IF no external locking or merge coordination is enabled
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate workspace
Pause one agent before the other writes shared files
Use git branches with manual merge review
Disable concurrent edits to the same repo
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: Open Interpreter can execute arbitrary code and modify files, while TREK is a real-time collaborative planner with AI built in. If TREK output is fed into Open Interpreter as authoritative text, Open Interpreter may act on incorrect travel facts or commands and then write or execute them. That is a direct A-to-B cascade with potentially irreversible side effects.
conditions: IF TREK output is used as input to Open Interpreter without verification
IF Open Interpreter is permitted to execute generated commands
IF the resulting actions modify files, bookings, or scripts
mitigations: Require human verification of TREK outputs before execution
Disable auto-run in Open Interpreter
Use a validation step for commands derived from TREK
Limit Open Interpreter to read-only review mode
requires-engineering: add schema validation for handoff messages

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly handles reservations, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, while Open Interpreter can access the entire local filesystem and send data to model providers. If regulated or personal travel data is stored in TREK and then read by Open Interpreter, residency and retention obligations can diverge. I cite both because the compliance risk arises from their interaction, not either agent alone.
conditions: IF TREK contains personal travel records or secrets subject to retention rules
IF Open Interpreter reads or transmits those records
IF the configured model provider or storage location has different residency or retention terms
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Open Interpreter inputs
Document a data-handling boundary between the tools
Use local inference for sensitive sessions
Review retention settings for TREK logs and uploads
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing by data class
